notes: The thousand names of Viṣṇu, taught by Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira (Mahābhārata, Anuśāsanaparvan, in the vulgate text Śaṅkara comments on): Yudhiṣṭhira's six questions and Bhīṣma's answer, the thousand names, and the fruit of reciting them. Meanings and translation follow Śaṅkara's bhāṣya.

provenance.source: The Works of Sri Sankaracharya, vol. 13, Sri Vani Vilas Press, Srirangam, 1910, pp. 1–170

sanskrit.deva:
श्रुत्वा धर्मानशेषेण पावनानि च सर्वशः ।
युधिष्ठिरः शान्तनवं पुनरेवाभ्यभाषत ॥ १ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
śrutvā dharmān aśeṣeṇa pāvanāni ca sarvaśaḥ |
yudhiṣṭhiraḥ śāntanavaṃ punar evābhyabhāṣata || 1 ||

lines.iast: śrutvā dharmān aśeṣeṇa pāvanāni ca sarvaśaḥ

padaccheda.iast: śrutvā dharmān aśeṣeṇa pāvanāni ca sarvaśaḥ yudhiṣṭhiraḥ śāntanavam punaḥ eva abhyabhāṣata
padaccheda.deva: श्रुत्वा धर्मान् अशेषेण पावनानि च सर्वशः युधिष्ठिरः शान्तनवम् पुनः एव अभ्यभाषत

translations.text: Having heard the dharmas without remainder, and the purifying (secrets of dharma) in every way, Yudhiṣṭhira spoke again to the son of Śantanu (Bhīṣma).

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the stotra, opens with three verses of his own: homage to Kṛṣṇa, whose form is being, consciousness and bliss, who does his work untiringly, who is known from the Vedānta, the teacher, the witness of the intellect; to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa, intent on the good of all beings, a sun to the lotus of the Veda, the dwelling of calm and the other virtues; and the hymn of the thousand names of Puruṣottama, of a thousand forms, with a thousand eyes, faces, feet and arms, is now explained, for the stilling of birth, old age and the rest.

Śaṅkara: Vaiśampāyana says this to Janamejaya. dharmān: the dharmas known by injunction, causes of prosperity and of the highest good; aśeṣeṇa: wholly; pāvanāni: those that destroy sin, the secrets of dharma; sarvaśaḥ: in every manner. Having heard them, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, asked Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, again, thinking that a means to every human end, easy to accomplish, needing little effort and bearing great fruit, had not yet been told.

sanskrit.deva:
किमेकं दैवतं लोके किं वाप्येकं परायणम् ।
स्तुवन्तः कं कमर्चन्तः प्राप्नुयुर्मानवाः शुभम् ॥ २ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
kim ekaṃ daivataṃ loke kiṃ vāpy ekaṃ parāyaṇam |
stuvantaḥ kaṃ kam arcantaḥ prāpnuyur mānavāḥ śubham || 2 ||

lines.iast: kim ekaṃ daivataṃ loke kiṃ vāpy ekaṃ parāyaṇam
lines.deva: किमेकं दैवतं लोके किं वाप्येकं परायणम्

lines.iast: stuvantaḥ kaṃ kam arcantaḥ prāpnuyur mānavāḥ śubham

padaccheda.iast: kim ekam daivatam loke kim vā api ekam parāyaṇam stuvantaḥ kam kam arcantaḥ prāpnuyuḥ mānavāḥ śubham
padaccheda.deva: किम् एकम् दैवतम् लोके किम् वा अपि एकम् परायणम् स्तुवन्तः कम् कम् अर्चन्तः प्राप्नुयुः मानवाः शुभम्

translations.text: What is the one deity in the world? And what is the one supreme goal? Praising whom, worshipping whom, would men gain the good?

notes: Śaṅkara: daivatam is deva, the suffix having its own sense. loke: in the world, that is, in all the branches of learning, which are the means of making things known (lokana): what is declared there as the one deity? That is the first question. parāyaṇam: the supreme place to be reached: by whose command all act; on reaching which the knot of the heart is cut (Muṇḍaka 2.2.9); by the mere knowing of which liberation, which is bliss, is gained; knowing which one fears nothing; entering which there is no rebirth; knowing which one becomes that very thing (‘he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman’, Muṇḍaka 3.2.9); apart from which men have no other path (Śvetāśvatara 3.8): what is that one goal? That is the second question.

Śaṅkara: praising which god, telling his qualities, and worshipping which god, with worship outer or inner of many kinds, would men, the sons of Manu, gain the good, the fruit of heaven, liberation and the rest? These are two more questions (the third and the fourth).

sanskrit.deva:
को धर्मः सर्वधर्माणां भवतः परमो मतः ।
किं जपन्मुच्यते जन्तुर्जन्मसंसारबन्धनात् ॥ ३ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
ko dharmaḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ bhavataḥ paramo mataḥ |
kiṃ japan mucyate jantur janmasaṃsārabandhanāt || 3 ||

lines.iast: ko dharmaḥ sarvadharmāṇāṃ bhavataḥ paramo mataḥ
lines.deva: को धर्मः सर्वधर्माणां भवतः परमो मतः

padaccheda.iast: kaḥ dharmaḥ sarva-dharmāṇām bhavataḥ paramaḥ mataḥ kim japan mucyate jantuḥ janma-saṃsāra-bandhanāt
padaccheda.deva: कः धर्मः सर्व-धर्माणाम् भवतः परमः मतः किम् जपन् मुच्यते जन्तुः जन्म-संसार-बन्धनात्

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. sg.

words.meaning: from the bond of birth and the round of birth

translations.text: Which dharma, of all dharmas, do you hold to be the highest? Repeating what is a creature freed from the bondage of birth and the round (of birth and death)?

notes: Śaṅkara: of all dharmas of the kind described, which is held by you to be the highest? That is the fifth question. japan: doing japa aloud, under the breath, or in the mind. jantu: one subject to birth; the word shows that all beings are entitled, as befits each, to japa, worship, praise and the rest. janma stands for all the effects that ignorance spreads out, saṃsāra for ignorance itself; freed from the bondage of these two: that is the sixth question. Being freed stands for the other fruits too; liberation is named to show that it is the chief.
Śaṅkara: six questions have been asked. Of them the sixth, the last, which is about what is to be repeated, is answered by the next verse.

sanskrit.deva:
जगत्प्रभुं देवदेवमनन्तं पुरुषोत्तमम् ।
स्तुवन्नामसहस्रेण पुरुषः सततोत्थितः ॥ ४ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
jagatprabhuṃ devadevam anantaṃ puruṣottamam |
stuvan nāmasahasreṇa puruṣaḥ satatotthitaḥ || 4 ||

padaccheda.iast: jagat-prabhum deva-devam anantam puruṣottamam stuvan nāma-sahasreṇa puruṣaḥ satata-utthitaḥ
padaccheda.deva: जगत्-प्रभुम् देव-देवम् अनन्तम् पुरुषोत्तमम् स्तुवन् नाम-सहस्रेण पुरुषः सतत-उत्थितः

translations.text: A man who, ever diligent, praises with the thousand names the lord of the world, the god of gods, the infinite, Puruṣottama, (goes beyond all sorrows).

notes: Śaṅkara: Bhīṣma, the cause of fear to all enemies outer and inner, the teacher of the Mokṣadharma and the rest, all-knowing, speaks. jagatprabhu: the master of the world, moving and unmoving. devadeva: the god of the gods, Brahmā and the others. ananta: not bounded by place, time or thing. puruṣottama: higher than the perishable and the imperishable, effect and cause. nāmasahasreṇa: with the thousand names, telling his qualities. satatotthitaḥ: constantly intent. puruṣa: so called from lying in the city (of the body), or from being full. ‘Goes beyond all sorrows’ (verse 6) is to be joined with each.

sanskrit.deva:
तमेव चार्चयन्नित्यं भक्त्या पुरुषमव्ययम् ।
ध्यायन्स्तुवन्नमस्यंश्च यजमानस्तमेव च ॥ ५ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
tam eva cārcayan nityaṃ bhaktyā puruṣam avyayam |
dhyāyan stuvan namasyaṃś ca yajamānas tam eva ca || 5 ||

lines.iast: tam eva cārcayan nityaṃ bhaktyā puruṣam avyayam
dhyāyan stuvan namasyaṃś ca yajamānas tam eva ca

padaccheda.iast: tam eva ca arcayan nityam bhaktyā puruṣam avyayam dhyāyan stuvan namasyan ca yajamānaḥ tam eva ca
padaccheda.deva: तम् एव च अर्चयन् नित्यम् भक्त्या पुरुषम् अव्ययम् ध्यायन् स्तुवन् नमस्यन् च यजमानः तम् एव च

translations.text: And the worshipper who always worships with devotion that same undecaying Puruṣa, meditating on him, praising him and bowing to him, (goes beyond all sorrows).

notes: Śaṅkara: this answers the fourth question. arcayan: doing outer worship, at all times; bhakti: devotion, being wholly intent on him; avyaya: free of destruction and change; dhyāyan: doing inner worship; stuvan and namasyan: praising him and bowing to him with the same devotion, praise and bowing being both parts of worship. yajamāna: the worshipper, who enjoys the fruit. Or arcayan names both kinds of worship, and meditating, praising and bowing are its mental, verbal and bodily forms.

sanskrit.deva:
अनादिनिधनं विष्णुं सर्वलोकमहेश्वरम् ।
लोकाध्यक्षं स्तुवन्नित्यं सर्वदुःखातिगो भवेत् ॥ ६ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
anādinidhanaṃ viṣṇuṃ sarvalokamaheśvaram |
lokādhyakṣaṃ stuvan nityaṃ sarvaduḥkhātigo bhavet || 6 ||

padaccheda.iast: anādi-nidhanam viṣṇum sarva-loka-maheśvaram loka-adhyakṣam stuvan nityam sarva-duḥkha-atigaḥ bhavet
padaccheda.deva: अनादि-निधनम् विष्णुम् सर्व-लोक-महेश्वरम् लोक-अध्यक्षम् स्तुवन् नित्यम् सर्व-दुःख-अतिगः भवेत्

words.meaning: the great lord of all the worlds

translations.text: Praising always Viṣṇu, who has no beginning or end, the great lord of all the worlds, the overseer of the world, one goes beyond all sorrows.

notes: Śaṅkara: the third question is answered by these three quarters. anādinidhana: free of the six changes of being. viṣṇu: the pervader. sarvalokamaheśvara: loka is what is seen, the visible world; he is lord even of Brahmā and the others who rule it. lokādhyakṣa: who sees the world directly by his own natural knowing. Praising him constantly, one goes beyond all sorrows, those of the body and the rest: this fruit is common to the three (verses 4–6).
The edition prints no number with this verse; it is the sixth.

sanskrit.deva:
ब्रह्मण्यं सर्वधर्मज्ञं लोकानां कीर्तिवर्धनम् ।
लोकनाथं महद्भूतं सर्वभूतभवोद्भवम् ॥ ७ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
brahmaṇyaṃ sarvadharmajñaṃ lokānāṃ kīrtivardhanam |
lokanāthaṃ mahad bhūtaṃ sarvabhūtabhavodbhavam || 7 ||

padaccheda.iast: brahmaṇyam sarva-dharma-jñam lokānām kīrti-vardhanam loka-nātham mahat bhūtam sarva-bhūta-bhava-udbhavam
padaccheda.deva: ब्रह्मण्यम् सर्व-धर्म-ज्ञम् लोकानाम् कीर्ति-वर्धनम् लोक-नाथम् महत् भूतम् सर्व-भूत-भव-उद्भवम्

words.meaning: from whom the becoming of all beings arises

translations.text: (Praising him) who is devoted to brahman, who knows all dharmas, who increases the fame of the worlds, the lord of the worlds, the great being, from whom the becoming of all beings arises.

notes: Śaṅkara: he further describes the one to be praised. brahmaṇya: good to brahman: to creation, to the brāhmaṇa, to austerity, or to the Veda. sarvadharmajña: who knows all dharmas. kīrtivardhana: who increases the fame of beings by entering them with his own power. lokanātha: he to whom the worlds pray, or who afflicts (upatapati), blesses or rules the worlds (the senses of nāth). mahad bhūtam: Brahman, great because it surpasses all, and being, the truth in the highest sense. sarvabhūtabhavodbhava: from whom arises the becoming, the round of birth and death, of all beings.

sanskrit.deva:
एष मे सर्वधर्माणां धर्मोऽधिकतमो मतः ।
यद्भक्त्या पुण्डरीकाक्षं स्तवैरर्चेन्नरः सदा ॥ ८ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
eṣa me sarvadharmāṇāṃ dharmo 'dhikatamo mataḥ |
yad bhaktyā puṇḍarīkākṣaṃ stavair arcen naraḥ sadā || 8 ||

lines.iast: yad bhaktyā puṇḍarīkākṣaṃ stavair arcen naraḥ sadā

padaccheda.iast: eṣaḥ me sarva-dharmāṇām dharmaḥ adhikatamaḥ mataḥ yat bhaktyā puṇḍarīka-akṣam stavaiḥ arcet naraḥ sadā
padaccheda.deva: एषः मे सर्व-धर्माणाम् धर्मः अधिकतमः मतः यत् भक्त्या पुण्डरीक-अक्षम् स्तवैः अर्चेत् नरः सदा

grammar.en: past passive participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: Of all dharmas this is held by me to be the highest dharma: that a man should always worship the lotus-eyed with devotion, by hymns.

notes: Śaṅkara: this answers the fifth question. Of all the dharmas known by injunction, this, about to be told, is in my view the highest: that a man always, with devotion, worships with hymns, praises that tell his qualities, the lotus-eyed, Vāsudeva, who shines in the lotus of the heart.

Śaṅkara, on why it is the highest: it needs no injury, no other person, no other material, no rule of place and time. So the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: ‘what one gains by meditation in the Kṛta age, by sacrifices in the Tretā, by worship in the Dvāpara, one gains in the Kali by praising Keśava’; Manu: ‘by japa alone a brāhmaṇa is fulfilled, there is no doubt; whether he does anything else or not, the friend (of all) is called a brāhmaṇa’; the Mahābhārata: ‘japa is called the highest dharma of all; the sacrifice of japa goes on without harm to beings’; and the Lord: ‘of sacrifices I am the sacrifice of japa’ (Gītā 10.25).

sanskrit.deva:
परमं यो महत्तेजः परमं यो महत्तपः ।
परमं यो महद्ब्रह्म परमं यः परायणम् ॥ ९ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
paramaṃ yo mahat tejaḥ paramaṃ yo mahat tapaḥ |
paramaṃ yo mahad brahma paramaṃ yaḥ parāyaṇam || 9 ||

lines.iast: paramaṃ yo mahat tejaḥ paramaṃ yo mahat tapaḥ
lines.deva: परमं यो महत्तेजः परमं यो महत्तपः

lines.iast: paramaṃ yo mahad brahma paramaṃ yaḥ parāyaṇam
lines.deva: परमं यो महद्ब्रह्म परमं यः परायणम्

padaccheda.iast: paramam yaḥ mahat tejaḥ paramam yaḥ mahat tapaḥ paramam yaḥ mahat brahma paramam yaḥ parāyaṇam
padaccheda.deva: परमम् यः महत् तेजः परमम् यः महत् तपः परमम् यः महत् ब्रह्म परमम् यः परायणम्

translations.text: He who is the supreme, great light; he who is the supreme, great ruling power; he who is the supreme, great Brahman; he who is the supreme goal: (he is the one goal of all beings).

notes: Śaṅkara: this settles the second question. tejas: the light that is consciousness, revealing all (‘by whose light the sun, kindled, burns’; ‘the gods worship him, the light of lights’; ‘there the sun does not shine’, Muṇḍaka 2.2.11; ‘the light that is in the sun’, Gītā 15.12). tapas: he who commands (tapati); his ruling of all is taught in the Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa (‘who, being within, rules this world, the other world and all beings’, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.7.1) and in the Taittirīya (‘from fear of him the wind blows’, 2.8); or tapati means ‘rules’ (īṣṭe); great, because his lordship is unbounded (‘he is the lord of all’). brahman: the supreme Brahman, truth and the rest, great as worthy of worship. parāyaṇa: the supreme goal, free of any doubt of return.

Śaṅkara: ‘supreme’ excludes the lower lights, the sun and the like. ‘Who’ is to be read each time as ‘the god who’: the god who is the supreme light, the supreme ruling power, the supreme Brahman, the supreme goal, he is the one goal of all beings: that is the sense of the sentence.

sanskrit.deva:
पवित्राणां पवित्रं यो मङ्गलानां च मङ्गलम् ।
दैवतं देवतानां च भूतानां योऽव्ययः पिता ॥ १० ॥
sanskrit.iast:
pavitrāṇāṃ pavitraṃ yo maṅgalānāṃ ca maṅgalam |
daivataṃ devatānāṃ ca bhūtānāṃ yo 'vyayaḥ pitā || 10 ||

lines.iast: pavitrāṇāṃ pavitraṃ yo maṅgalānāṃ ca maṅgalam
lines.deva: पवित्राणां पवित्रं यो मङ्गलानां च मङ्गलम्

lines.iast: daivataṃ devatānāṃ ca bhūtānāṃ yo 'vyayaḥ pitā
lines.deva: दैवतं देवतानां च भूतानां योऽव्ययः पिता

padaccheda.iast: pavitrāṇām pavitram yaḥ maṅgalānām ca maṅgalam daivatam devatānām ca bhūtānām yaḥ avyayaḥ pitā
padaccheda.deva: पवित्राणाम् पवित्रम् यः मङ्गलानाम् च मङ्गलम् दैवतम् देवतानाम् च भूतानाम् यः अव्ययः पिता

translations.text: He who is the purifier of purifiers, the auspicious of auspicious things, the deity of deities, the undecaying father of beings: (he is the one deity in the world).

notes: Śaṅkara: this answers the first question. pavitrāṇāṃ pavitram: the purifier of the things that purify, holy places and the rest; for the supreme Puruṣa, meditated on, seen, named, praised, worshipped, remembered and bowed to, roots out all sins; or he destroys, by the knowledge of his true nature, the action of merit and demerit that causes the bondage of the round, and ignorance, its cause. He supports this with many verses of the Purāṇas and Itihāsas on the power of meditating on Hari and naming him (‘naming Keśava in the Kali age’; ‘as fire to metals, so the naming of him with devotion to all sins’; ‘even one bow to Kṛṣṇa equals ten horse sacrifices; the one who sacrificed returns to birth, the one who bowed to Kṛṣṇa does not’, and others). maṅgalānāṃ maṅgalam: maṅgala is happiness, its means and what makes it known; he is the supreme good, whose nature is the highest bliss. daivataṃ devatānām: the god of gods, surpassing them in shining and the rest. bhūtānāṃ avyayaḥ pitā: the undecaying father of beings. The god who is these is the one deity in the world: that is the sense of the sentence.

Śaṅkara, on there being one god: ‘one god, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings’ (Śvetāśvatara 6.11); ‘one only, without a second’ (Chāndogya 6.2.1). If it is said that there cannot be one god since the jīva and the supreme differ: no, scripture teaches that the supreme, unchanged, entered as the witness of the intellect and its states (‘having created it, he entered it’, Taittirīya 2.6; ‘he has entered here, to the tips of the nails’, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.7). If it is said that those who entered differ among themselves: no, it is the one who is heard of as entering in many ways (‘one god, settled in many ways’; ‘as the one fire, entering the world, takes the form of each thing’, Kaṭha 2.2.9–10; ‘one truth the sages call by many names’, Ṛgveda 1.164.46). So the Upaniṣads, the Gītā (‘who worships me as dwelling in all beings, resting in oneness’, 6.31; ‘I am the Self seated in the heart of all beings’, 10.20), the Harivaṃśa, Manu, and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (‘I, you and all this are the Self; give up the delusion of difference’) and other Purāṇas, where Maheśvara says that those who see him as other than Hari sin, and that there is no difference between Hari and himself.

Śaṅkara, on the same: ‘they acknowledge him as the Self and make it known’ (Brahmasūtra 4.1.3). The Jābālas take him as the Self, ‘I am you, O god, and you are I’; and the Vedānta teaches him as the Self (‘he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal’; ‘that is the Self; that you are’). This is not a symbol-view, like seeing Viṣṇu in an image: that would make the teaching figurative, and in a symbol-view the statement is made once, ‘the mind is Brahman’, whereas here it is made both ways, ‘you are I, I am you’. And seeing difference is condemned (‘he who worships another deity, thinking “he is one, I am another”, does not know’, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10; ‘he goes from death to death who sees as if there were difference here’, Kaṭha 2.1.10), while seeing oneness is taught as right knowledge (Gītā 4.35, 18.20). Even on the view that ignorance is the limiting adjunct, scripture and tradition bear it out: the difference of Self and Brahman is made by ignorance and ends with it, as the many spaces of pots are one space; ‘the manifold is mere mind; non-duality is the highest truth’ (Gauḍapāda).

Śaṅkara, on the authority of the Veda: the Veda is a valid source also for what already exists, the Self, and not only for what is to be done; words convey meanings related to one another, not only to something to be done, or the arthavāda passages would not connect; it is desire that moves one to act, not the injunction (‘as is his desire, so is his will; as his will, so his deed’, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.5; Manu 2.4). Mantras and arthavādas are valid even where their aim is something else: Nahuṣa, who denied the authority of the mantras for the sprinkling of cows and kicked Agastya, became a serpent (Mahābhārata). So the knowledge of the Self is to be received with faith (Gītā 9.3; the Aitareya: ‘this is the path, this the work, this Brahman, this the truth; let one not neglect it’, with the ṛc ‘three races went beyond’, those who went beyond becoming trees, plants and creeping things; ‘those who slay the Self go to the sunless worlds’, Īśa 3; ‘he who knows Brahman as non-existent becomes non-existent’, Taittirīya 2.6; ‘what sin has he not done, the thief who steals the Self, who takes the Self to be other than it is?’, the story of Śakuntalā).

Śaṅkara, on bathing fit for the japa of the thousand names: the bath in the tīrtha of the mind, in which the gods, the Vedas and all that purifies become one; the lake of knowledge with the water of meditation, which washes away the dirt of attachment and aversion (Mahābhārata); ‘the bath of the mind is the thinking of Viṣṇu’ (Viṣṇusmṛti); ‘pure or impure, in whatever state, he who remembers the lotus-eyed is pure within and without’.
The edition prints no number with this verse; it is the tenth.

sanskrit.deva:
यतः सर्वाणि भूतानि भवन्त्यादियुगागमे ।
यस्मिंश्च प्रलयं यान्ति पुनरेव युगक्षये ॥ ११ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
yataḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni bhavanty ādiyugāgame |
yasmiṃś ca pralayaṃ yānti punar eva yugakṣaye || 11 ||

lines.iast: yasmiṃś ca pralayaṃ yānti punar eva yugakṣaye

padaccheda.iast: yataḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni bhavanti ādi-yuga-āgame yasmin ca pralayam yānti punaḥ eva yuga-kṣaye
padaccheda.deva: यतः सर्वाणि भूतानि भवन्ति आदि-युग-आगमे यस्मिन् च प्रलयम् यान्ति पुनः एव युग-क्षये

words.meaning: at the coming of the first age
at the end of the age

translations.text: From whom all beings come into being at the coming of the first age, and in whom alone they go again to dissolution at the end of the age;

notes: Śaṅkara: the one deity just set forth is now marked out. yugakṣaye: at the great dissolution. eva: in him alone, in no other. ca: and in whom they stand in between (‘that from which these beings are born’, Taittirīya 3.1).

sanskrit.deva:
तस्य लोकप्रधानस्य जगन्नाथस्य भूपते ।
विष्णोर्नामसहस्रं मे शृणु पापभयापहम् ॥ १२ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
tasya lokapradhānasya jagannāthasya bhūpate |
viṣṇor nāmasahasraṃ me śṛṇu pāpabhayāpaham || 12 ||

padaccheda.iast: tasya loka-pradhānasya jagat-nāthasya bhūpate viṣṇoḥ nāma-sahasram me śṛṇu pāpa-bhaya-apaham
padaccheda.deva: तस्य लोक-प्रधानस्य जगत्-नाथस्य भूपते विष्णोः नाम-सहस्रम् मे शृणु पाप-भय-अपहम्

words.meaning: which takes away sin and fear

translations.text: Hear from me, O king, the thousand names of that Viṣṇu, the chief of the worlds, the lord of the world, which take away sin and fear.

notes: Śaṅkara: of the one deity so marked; lokapradhāna: set forth as chief by the branches of learning, the means of making the world known; jagannātha: the master of the worlds, the supreme Self, who wields māyā and yet is untouched; bhūpate: O king; viṣṇu: whose nature is to pervade. The thousand names destroy sin and fear; hear them from me with one-pointed mind, and hold them. The Viṣṇudharma says that the names have different powers, and different fruits are gained by uttering them.

Śaṅkara, on how words name him: in the supreme Brahman there are no relation, quality, action, genus or convention, the grounds on which words apply; yet in Brahman with qualities and with modifications, being the Self of all, these grounds are found, so all words apply to the supreme Puruṣa.

sanskrit.deva:
यानि नामानि गौणानि विख्यातानि महात्मनः ।
ऋषिभिः परिगीतानि तानि वक्ष्यामि भूतये ॥ १३ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
yāni nāmāni gauṇāni vikhyātāni mahātmanaḥ |
ṛṣibhiḥ parigītāni tāni vakṣyāmi bhūtaye || 13 ||

padaccheda.iast: yāni nāmāni gauṇāni vikhyātāni mahātmanaḥ ṛṣibhiḥ parigītāni tāni vakṣyāmi bhūtaye
padaccheda.deva: यानि नामानि गौणानि विख्यातानि महात्मनः ऋषिभिः परिगीतानि तानि वक्ष्यामि भूतये

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. pl.
past passive participle n. nom. pl.

translations.text: The names of the great Self that are drawn from his qualities, well known, sung everywhere by the seers: those I shall tell, for well-being (the four human ends).

notes: Śaṅkara: gauṇāni: arising from his qualities, applied because of qualities; among them those that are well known, sung everywhere by the seers, seers of mantras and those who know them, in the accounts of the supreme Lord. mahātman: great and the Self; ‘because it obtains, takes, eats the objects here, and because its being is unbroken, it is called ātman’; he alone is the great Self, of unthinkable power. bhūtaye: for the gaining of the four human ends, for those who seek them.

Śaṅkara, before the names: words like āditya, whose usual sense is another, still praise him in the thousand names, since those things are his glories and not other than he (‘the elements, the senses, Prakṛti, the self and the supreme Self: you alone stand fivefold’, Viṣṇu Purāṇa; Gītā 10.21–42; ‘Puruṣa alone is all this’, Muṇḍaka 2.1.10). A name that comes again, like viṣṇu, is no repetition, for it is taken in another sense by another derivation; names like śrīpati and mādhava, alike in sense, differ in word; and even sameness of sense is no fault, since the question was about one deity. Where a word is masculine, ‘Viṣṇu’ is understood; where feminine, ‘the deity’; where neuter, ‘Brahman’.
